content: Discussion thread for #Project announcements > Computable smith form of matrices over Euclidean Domains

Nice! This is an essential component!

As I've been talking about in #Computer algebra > Active projects, I think it's important we have implementations like this that don't rely on Mathlib. (i.e. the computational part doesn't use Mathlib, then there's a downstream library connecting it to all the Mathlib theory).

This allows people to use the computational part even if Mathlib is too big an import, and also leaves open the path for these tools to eventually be used in Mathlib.
I cannot tell you how happy it makes me when someone posts a project with the word computable in Lean :)

Aren't there some definitions (or other computable functions) that you'd want to write, but which do rely on theorems in Mathlib for their definitions? (I have no concrete examples in mind, but it seems to me you're likely to end up duplicating a lot of things from Mathlib)

Many definitions in Mathlib are not optimized for computational efficiency, but rather for "theoretical efficiency". Representations that are easy to reason about / prove with, instead of easy / fast to compute with.

Right now my project does depend on mathlib (necessarily, since it includes theorems that relate my implementation with mathlib's). I guess it would be possible to refactor it into two parts: one with the implementation and no "hard" theorems (just the ones that prove that you are not accessing an array ot of bounds, and similar things), and one with the theorems about the properties of the result (that would depend on mathlib).

I am not sure right now how much work this refactoring would require, since I haven't worried about avoiding mathlib in the purely computable part.

Johan Commelin said:

Many definitions in Mathlib are not optimized for computational efficiency, but rather for "theoretical efficiency". Representations that are easy to reason about / prove with, instead of easy / fast to compute with.

I found that the hard way: my first approach was to use Mathlib's matrices (which are internally functions). But then the complexity of the matrices exploded, since the product of several concrete matrices (or applying several elementary operations to a matrix) became a composition of many functions, without doing any reduction.
In my recent experience keeping two separate repos is pretty painless, but I'm relying on AIs to do all the busywork of actually typing characters into files and keeping repos in sync. :-)
